[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining. we're gonna do a deep dive on the runtime perf stuff you flagged, especially around the MoE model routing costs and rope scaling across the Qwen and Mistral family. Camille is gonna kick off with runtime notes.
[00:18] Camille: yeah thanks jordan. hi team. quick agenda, we'll cover kernel selection, kv cache, batching heuristics, then quantization, then specific model notes for llama / mistral / qwen and then moE routing costs.
[00:30] Samir: great, thanks. our main constraints: sub-50ms p50 for short chat messages, 99th under 300ms, and cost needs to be below our current infra baseline.
[00:42] Maya: and we want to try private deployment (VPC) for PII data, so any notes about KMS and HSM are very relevant.
[00:50] Camille: noted. quick caveat: some product names get munged in our transcript - apologies if i say rope but mean RoPE, small typos.
[01:05] Alex: starting with kernel selection: our runtime does architecture-aware kernel picking. for Llama-like models with causal attention we prefer fused attention kernels at short seq lengths (<=512) to get lower latency. for Mistral the attention layout is a bit different so we pick kernels optimized for grouped matmuls. for Qwen we've seen better throughputs with matmul tiling tuned for its larger hidden dims.
[01:42] Diego: quick q - how deterministic is kernel selection? we want repeatable perf across restarts.
[01:48] Camille: selection is deterministic given model shape + hw + sequence length distribution, but if the underlying cudnn/cuda lib versions change you can see different kernels pick. we log kernel choices in the trace so you can replay.
[02:12] Lina: on KV cache, we observed that Mistral's kv layout has bigger per-token memory overhead compared to Llama for same hidden size, is that correct?
[02:20] Alex: yes, Mistral tends to materialize slightly larger KV due to its attention projection shape; that increases memory pressure and changes batching sweet spots.
[02:32] Camille: practical tip: for models with larger KV per token, raising batch size too much can force GPU memory spills; we prefer smaller batch sizes plus smarter continuous batching (low-latency interleaving) to keep p50 low.
[02:50] Samir: can you explain continuous batching again, we've seen standard batching cause tail latency spikes.
[02:57] Camille: sure — continuous batching groups inflight requests on micro-batches and uses a deadline policy: either X tokens or Y ms threshold. that prevents long waits. also we use prefix KV caching so repeated prompt prefixes skip compute.
[03:18] Samir: how warm does the KV cache need to be to meet our 99th?
[03:24] Camille: depends. if most queries share a 128-token prefix, cache hits are super fast. worst case cold starts for long context windows (2k-4k) can add 40-120ms depending on model and quantization.
[03:38] Maya: about quantization, we run QAT and PTQ experiments. which quant profiles are safe for these models?
[03:44] Alex: FP16 is the default for inference. int8 (LLM.int8) works for many Llama variants with minor quality drop, but Qwen tends to be more sensitive to aggressive int8 block quantization - we've seen hallucination/score shifts in some evals.
[04:05] Lina: any guidance on mixed quant, like keeping attention and layernorm in fp16 and quantizing feedforward?
[04:11] Camille: exactly. the common pattern: keep attention kernels and layernorm in fp16, quantize matmuls in feedforward to 8-bit. that gives big memory/cost wins with smaller quality delta. we will share a quantization matrix.
[04:27] Jordan: moving to MoE: Helix mentioned interest in sparsely activated experts to reduce FLOPs. Camille, can you outline runtime overheads?
[04:36] Camille: MoE reduces compute when sparsity is high but introduces routing overheads: gather/scatter ops, additional memory for expert parameters, and load imbalance. routing also hurts batching because the active expert set varies per request.
[04:54] Samir: so is MoE net beneficial for latency-sensitive workloads?
[04:58] Camille: for throughput-oriented batch jobs yes. for low-latency chat with strict 99th targets it's tricky: routing adds jitter. our tests show MoE gives cost win at >2k tokens per request or very high concurrency where you can amortize routing costs. for small chat messages, Dense with quant works better.
[05:20] Diego: can routing be pinned to a subset of experts to reduce jitter?
[05:24] Alex: you can implement constrained routing or sticky routing heuristics to increase cache locality but that reduces expressivity. it's a tradeoff—Helix might accept slight quality loss for deterministic perf.
[05:36] Maya: about RoPE scaling — Qwen claims RoPE scaling fixes long-context drift. we've seen some alignment drift with Llama at long sequences. what's the runtime impact?
[05:48] Camille: RoPE scaling changes attention computation; some implementations require recomputing rotary embeddings on the fly for very long contexts which adds CPU overhead if not optimized. we offload rotary precompute to GPU kernels when possible. Qwen's implementation is heavier but gives better long-context numeric stability.
[06:10] Lina: does that alter KV size?
[06:12] Alex: not significantly in terms of bytes, but the compute per token rises slightly due to extra trig-like ops or ember rotation math. our kernel picks account for that.
[06:23] Samir: can you give ballpark numbers comparing p50/p99 for a 128-token chat across models (dense + fp16, batch size = 8, on a single A100)?
[06:33] Camille: rough numbers: Llama-2-13B dense FP16 p50 ~ 38ms, p99 ~ 180ms; Mistral-7B dense FP16 p50 ~ 30ms, p99 ~ 120ms (but larger KV per token); Qwen-14B dense FP16 p50 ~ 45ms, p99 ~ 220ms. With int8 quant we see 20-30% p50 improvements but p99 improvements are smaller unless we also tune batching deadlines.
[07:02] Samir: interesting — Qwen p99 looks worse. is that quant sensitivity or kernel mismatch?
[07:07] Alex: mix of both. Qwen's larger dims lead to less favorable small-batch matmul tiling, so tail latency gets worse. we mitigate via hot-path kernel tuning and some heuristic pre-batching for common prompt sizes.
[07:24] Maya: for VPC/on-prem, are there kernel limitations compared to Redwood Hosted?
[07:31] Camille: we support identical runtime in Private as long as the GPU driver stack and CUDA/cuDNN versions are consistent. some specialized kernels require specific microcode; we'll provide a checklist for kernel compatibility. KMS/HSM: we integrate with customer KMS via our private control plane and support HSM-backed keys for models and logs.
[07:50] Diego: do you support isolated hardware tenancy for compliance?
[07:53] Jordan: yes, Dedicated or on-prem gives isolated GPU pools and network isolation; we can map SR-IOV and restrict egress.
[08:02] Samir: regarding benchmarks, can you run the same prompt set in our VPC for apples-to-apples?
[08:07] Camille: yes, we can run a 48-hour window of stress tests and tail-latency captures in your VPC. we'll need your prompt set and a target concurrency map.
[08:17] Jordan: quick interjection — note that some product names may be transcribed slightly off, we'll attach the perf sheets after.
[08:26] Samir: ok thanks. on MoE costs—can you share numbers for memory overhead per expert and routing percent overhead?
[08:33] Alex: ballpark: each expert adds its parameter size (so 2x-4x parameter overhead depending on routing policy), runtime routing overhead ~5-20% extra compute per token when active due to gather/scatter. load imbalance can spike that further.
[08:51] Lina: any suggestions to reduce load imbalance?
[08:53] Camille: use capacity factoring, expert dropout during training, or adaptive routing that considers expert load. those are model changes though; runtime can do batching heuristics to group same-expert requests.
[09:07] Maya: curious about fallback policies — you mentioned automatic fallback to compatible model variants when capacity constrained. how does that affect quality and user experience?
[09:16] Jordan: we implement policy-based routing: if dedicated pool is saturated we can route to a smaller or quantized variant with a quality tag. customer controls thresholds and can set canary rules for specific tenants.
[09:28] Samir: would routing add request latency spikes?
[09:31] Camille: there's usually a small routing decision latency (~2-8ms) but the biggest concern is warming the alternative model; cached warm instances mitigate that.
[09:40] Diego: what's the logging/trace fidelity? we need per-request kernel picks and expert routing decisions for audits.
[09:47] Alex: we log kernel selection, batch composition, kv hit/miss, routing expert choices and quant profile used. logs are retained per your retention policy and can be exported to your SIEM.
[09:59] Lina: small nit — we've seen rope exponent drift in long sequence numerical tests with Llama. any tuned patches?
[10:06] Camille: yes there are RoPE scaling patches that adjust the frequency schedule to avoid high-frequency attenuation. Qwen uses a different schedule which is more stable at 16k+. we can share patch diffs and perf impact.
[10:22] Samir: can you summarize recommended configs per model for Helix's chat use case (short messages, high tail requirements)?
[10:28] Camille: recommended:
- Llama-2-13B: Dense FP16 + smart batching, prefix KV enabled, batch size 6-12, int8 only after eval; good p50 but watch p99.
- Mistral-7B: Dense FP16 preferred, slightly smaller batch sizes (4-8), KV cache warm strategy to avoid spills.
- Qwen-14B: Dense FP16 but requires kernel tuning; consider mixed quant with conservative int8. avoid MoE for low-latency chat.
- MoE: only for high-throughput generative workloads; not recommended for strict p99 targets.
